articleTitle: Presidential address
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The honour which this Institute has bestowed upon me by electing me as its President carries with it many obligations, not the least of which is the duty of giving a Presidential Address. When considering a possible subject for this address I stopped to wonder why a Presidential Address is expected, and came to the conclusion that it is in order to give the President an opportunity to expound on his favourite theme or subject; in other words, the Presidential Address is expected to be personal rather than impersonal and technical.

articleTitle: Earth leakage protection schemes and relays
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In view of the fact that faults to earth represent the most frequent type of failure to which electrical apparatus is subject, an earth leakage protective system fulfils a most important function and localises the trouble by rapid isolation of the faulty apparatus. The core balance and residual current systems of earth leakage protection were discussed in a paper entitled “Neutral Earthing and Earth Leakage Protection” in this Journal for March, 1940, and the object of the present paper is to consider various specialised forms of protection for particular types of apparatus.

articleTitle: War Emergency cables
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Advice has been received from the South African Cable Makers' Association that owing to War developments and in agree ment with the British Government, all future shipments of rubber insulated cables from Great Britain will contain a smaller rubber content than has been the standard with British manufacturers in the past. The thickness of insulation will re main as at present standardised, but owing to the lower rubber contents in the insula tion it follows that the tests to which cables may be placed will be correspond ingly affected.

abstract: The President: Gentlemen, I regret that my first duty this evening is to deal with obituary notices, and in this respect refer to the passing of:�Mr. L. B. Woodworth, a Foundation Member of the Institute, who was President in 1921, elected an Honorary Member in 1939, and died at Durban on the 29th May, 1942. An obituary notice appeared in the June issue of the Transactions. Mr. P. Herd (Member), who was very well known in Johannesburg and district, joined the Institute in 1910, and died on the 20th August, 1942. Mr. A. E. Scott (Retired Member), joined the Institute originally in 1909, and died at Capetown on the' 24th July, 1942. Mr. H. C. Cook (Associate Member), joined the Institute in 1935, and died at Aliwal North this month. Mr. K. T. Robinson (Associate), joined the Institute in 1940, and died at Schweizer Reneke on the 5th March, 1942.

articleTitle: Field testing of high voltage bushings
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The defects which occur in condenser type bushings are discussed and examples of the consequences of unchecked deterioration are given. Methods of detecting such defects in their incipient stage are considered.

articleTitle: Electrical applications in aircraft
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Some three decades ago the aeroplane was a comparatively small and simple machine in which electrical circuits — apart from engine ignition — were nonexistent. The enormous advance in the design of aircraft made since these early days would never have been possible had not electricity been called upon to a greater and greater extent to perform innumerable functions, which not only facilitated but permitted the modern aeroplane to take the air with the full confidence of its crew.

abstract: The last duty which befalls me as an outgoing President of this Institute is to present an address in the form of a valediction. It has been said that “they also serve who only stand and wait.” To these words I hasten to add “and sit and listen”!

articleTitle: Crosstalk on south african telephone lines
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In the Union of South Africa the development of the communication network depends on the extensive use of carrier telephone systems which operate over open wire metallic circuits for distances up to a maximum of 1,000 miles. The range of frequencies employed extends to 150 kilocycles per second, and the successful operation of the systems at these high frequencies depends almost entirely on the attenuation, crosstalk and impedance characteristics of the open wire routes.

articleTitle: Power interference in communication circuits in South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: I think the authors are to be congratu lated upon a paper of exceptional interest. It is unusual in papers on telephone inter ference to find the power and telephone aspects of the problem both so adequately dealt with and balance in the same paper and this fact alone will make this a valuable work of reference. Still more useful, however, is the much overdue clarification which the authors have brought about regarding the causes of the telephone interference experienced in the particular cases of the Natal and Eeef systems.
